title: GraphQL Client Caching — Handwritten Deep Dive
summary: A 10-page dense-notes carousel on how GraphQL clients cache data: normalized store internals, Apollo Client and urql patterns, fragments, and cache updates after mutations.

chapters.title: Why GraphQL Caching Is Different
points: REST caches live at the URL level; GraphQL sends everything to one endpoint, so HTTP caching fails by default
A GraphQL response is a graph — the same object can appear at multiple paths (e.g. viewer and post.author)
Without normalization, two copies of one entity drift apart when one is updated
Document caching (full responses keyed by query+variables) vs normalized caching (entities keyed by id)
Client cache is the single source of truth for the UI: components read from cache, not raw fetch responses
Three jobs of a client cache: store results, deduplicate entities, serve/refresh on re-render
Trade-off: normalization buys consistency and reuse, costs implementation complexity
Cache hits skip the network entirely — the biggest perceived-performance win
GraphQL spec itself defines no caching; it's entirely the client's job
Tools in this handbook: Apollo Client 3 and urql 3+ (both normalized or near-normalized)
Cost model: naive caching = O(responses); normalized = O(entities), usually far fewer objects
Rule of thumb: cache per-entity, not per-query

chapters.title: Normalization Internals
points: Normalization: flatten the response graph into a map of entities keyed by `TypeName:id`
Example: { "User:1": { id: 1, name: "Ada" } } — references stored as { __ref: "User:1" }
Default ID computation: `__typename + id`, or `__typename + _id`; composite keys for types lacking unique ids
Response walker: client traverses result objects, replaces embedded objects with references, writes into store
Repeating entities across queries merge into one entity via field-by-field shallow merge — no delete of missing fields
Reading: query is re-walked against the store, references dereferenced back into a tree
Cache misses on a field while reading → the read fails or returns partial data depending on policy
Memory shape: two top-level maps — entities (data) and root/query results metadata
Why shallow merge matters: a list query returning partial user fields won't erase fields written by a fuller query
Complexity: write O(fields in response), read O(fields in query) — independent of how many times the entity appears
Garbage collection: Apollo's `gc()` removes entities unreachable from active roots; `retain()/release()` pin objects
Key gotcha: two different server types sharing an id (e.g. Comment:1 vs User:1) are safe — typename is in the key

chapters.title: Apollo Client Setup & Data Sources
points: Core pieces: ApolloClient + InMemoryCache + HttpLink; create once, pass via ApolloProvider
`new InMemoryCache({ typePolicies })` is the central config surface
useQuery returns { data, loading, error }; refetch, fetchMore, startPolling, subscribeToMore
Fetch policies: cache-first (default), cache-and-network, network-only, no-cache, cache-only
Fetch policy is per-query and overridable — `nextFetchPolicy` switches after first fetch
useLazyQuery for on-demand execution; useMutation returns a tuple [mutate, result]
useReactiveQuery/useFragment for surgical reads — read one entity without subscribing to a whole query
Client-only fields via @client directive and local resolvers: cache doubles as local state store
Identifiers in setup: `new InMemoryCache({ dataIdFromObject })` as legacy alternative to typePolicies.keyFields
DevTools: Apollo Client Devtools shows cache contents, query history, mutation writes
Suspense mode and `skip` for conditional queries
Common mistake: creating the client inside a component → cache recreated every render

chapters.title: Type Policies & Custom Keys
points: typePolicies: per-__typename config for keys, fields, and relationships
keyFields: ['id'] default; composite `keyFields: ['id', 'slug']`; keyFields: false disables normalization for a type
Nested key fields: `keyFields: ['author', ['id']]` when the key lives inside a nested object
When the server id isn't the cache key: keyFields with a function or custom read for the field
fields map configures caching behavior of individual fields
merge functions: `merge(existing, incoming)` control how field values combine on repeated writes
Classic use: pagination fields — merge concat pages in order, dedupe by cursor
Pagination helpers: `keyArgs` (which args make distinct cache entries) + offset/relay-style merge recipes
read functions: compute field values on the fly (e.g. derived fullName) without storing them
read/write pairs enable client-side schema extensions
Risk: custom merge fns must be pure and return new values — mutating `existing` corrupts the cache
Mistake: forgetting keyArgs → different filter args overwrite each other's results

chapters.title: Fragments: Reuse & Cache Colocation
points: Fragment = named, reusable selection set spread into queries/mutations with `...FragmentName`
Colocation pattern: each component owns its fragment; parent queries spread children's fragments
Cache payoff: a component's data needs are declared once and shared across every query that uses it
useFragment(cacheId, fragment) reads and live-subscribes to exactly one entity's fields
Inline fragments + type conditions for unions/interfaces: `... on Admin { permissions }`
Cache reads of interfaces return concrete __typename — cache stores the concrete entity
Fragment matching with @defer / streamed partial results: cache fills in as chunks arrive
Apollo fragment registry tools (graphql-codegen `documents`, fragment masking in newer versions)
Fragment masking: components see only their fragment's fields — improves type safety, hides query shape
Pitfall: fragments never requested by any query are never cached
Pitfall: fragment on an interface without type conditions may fetch fields the server rejects
Rule: fetch with queries, think in fragments

chapters.title: Mutation Cache Updates
points: Four update strategies: (1) automatic normalization update, (2) refetchQueries, (3) update() manual write, (4) cache.modify
Automatic: if the mutation returns an entity with __typename+id, merged fields just appear — prefer designing mutations to return affected entities
refetchQueries: string names or documents; runs after mutation resolves; simple but costs extra round trips
awaitRefetchQueries + optimisticResponse interplay: optimistic result visible before refetch completes
update(cache, { data }) reads the mutation result and writes derived changes with cache.writeQuery / writeFragment
Pattern: read the list with a fragment, insert/update/delete the entity, write back
Typical delete: read parent's list fragment, filter out the id, write back — plus consider orphans left in cache
cache.evict({ id, fieldName }) removes entity/field; cache.gc() then sweeps unreferenced entities
cache.modify reads raw store values (with toReference/readField) for surgical field edits without refetch
Rules of update(): never throw on missing data (partial cache), keep it idempotent
Anti-pattern: manually mirroring server-computed values — write operations that shift state, not compute it
Choosing: normalized auto-update first, evict for deletes, update() for lists/aggregates, refetch as safety net

chapters.title: Optimistic UI
points: optimisticResponse: fake mutation result applied to cache immediately, replaced by server truth later
Must match the mutation's shape exactly, including __typename and id, or the optimistic write lands nowhere
Works with update(): update() runs once per optimistic layer and again with real data
Apollo implements this as a cache layer: optimistic layers stack, `rollback` pops them on error
onQueryUpdated(cacheObj, diff) — react to entities the mutation touched (e.g. auto-evict stale ones)
Failure path: layer removed → cache reverts automatically; UI must handle the error state (toast/rollback)
Concurrent mutations: multiple optimistic layers order-stacked; interleaved reads see combined state
urql equivalent: no built-in optimistic layer — use optimistic updates via custom exchange or manual write in updaters
Use for likes/votes/toggles; avoid for payments or anything needing server validation before UI commitment
Keep optimistic payloads minimal — only fields the UI immediately renders
Gotcha: server-computed fields (createdAt, ids) must be faked plausibly or UI flickers when replaced
Testing: simulate mutation rejection to verify rollback UX

chapters.title: urql Patterns
points: urql core: Client + exchanges (composable middleware for operations) — fetching, dedup, caching are all exchanges
Default document cache: hashes query+variables as key, stores whole responses — fast, no normalization
Document cache invalidation by typing: any mutation result containing a typename invalidates all queries touching that typename
Simple but coarse: one mutation on User invalidates every User query → frequent refetches
@urql/exchange-graphcache adds full normalization: same keys as Apollo (`id`/`_id` default, configurable schema keys)
graphcache config: updates (mutation handlers), resolvers (read-time computed), keys, optimistic (sync fn per mutation)
updates.For Mutation type: `Mutation.addTodo(result, args, cache, info)` writes via cache.link/writeFragment
Optimistic in graphcache: `optimistic: { addTodo(...) }` returns a fake result synchronously
Suspense mode, request policies (cache-first/cache-and-network) mirror Apollo's policies with different names
Comparison: urql lighter (~smaller bundle, simpler mental model), Apollo richer tooling + ecosystem
When to pick urql: smaller apps or document cache suffices; Apollo: large normalized apps, codegen, devtools
Both share the same mental model — learn one, transfer to the other

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Pitfalls & Review
points: Consistency risk: manual update() bugs create phantom state — prefer server-truth responses and evict+gc
Cache staleness is invisible: Apollo has no TTL by default; use cache-and-network or refetch on focus (refetchOnWindowFocus patterns, urql staleness flag)
Memory growth: long sessions accumulate entities — schedule gc(), retain pinned objects deliberately
Debugging toolkit: inspect normalized store (not the response) — the cache is the UI's data source
Common bug #1: types missing unique id → every object cached separately, dedup silently broken
Common bug #2: mutation returns nothing normalized → UI 'doesn't update' though mutation succeeded
Common bug #3: pagination merges colliding across different args (missing keyArgs)
Common bug #4: update() reading a query never fetched → cache.readQuery returns null, crashes the update
Performance note: cache reads are synchronous & cheap; re-renders come from query subscriptions, use useFragment/useMemo to scope them
SSR/hydration: serialize cache (extract()) to the client and restore to avoid double fetches
Checklist: keyFields correct? mutations return entities? deletes evict? lists have merges+keyArgs? optimistic rollback tested?
Mental model to keep: normalized entity map + references; every read/write walks that map
